title: Come unto me (Matthew 11:25–30)
hook: a week too heavy, and an invitation to take on a yoke
tomorrow: what do you do with something that's already cracked?

segments.voice: Yesterday, kids in a market who wouldn't dance or mourn, and two complaints that cancel out. Dance when they play. Now, what to do when you're too tired to dance at all.

Two tests, a shift, rehearsal every night, and a phone that buzzes through dinner. Some weeks the list is longer than the week. Here's the surprise in Jesus' answer to heavy. He doesn't say: put everything down. He says: take my yoke. A yoke is a wooden beam that sits across the necks of working animals so they can pull together. It's the gear of work, not of rest. So Christians read his offer in more than one way.
screen: `THE LIST IS LONGER THAN THE WEEK.` → `NOT 'PUT IT DOWN.'` → `TAKE MY YOKE.`

segments.voice: Here are his words, in the King James: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light." One reading leans on the first sentence. Rest is a gift: I will give you rest. Nobody earns it. You come tired, as you are, and it's handed to you. Just before this, Jesus thanks his Father for showing these things to babes, not to the wise and prudent, and babes don't earn anything. Another reading leans on the second sentence. Take my yoke, and learn of me. A yoke is still a yoke. The rest comes from pulling beside a gentle teacher, learning his pace, not from never pulling again. On this reading, rest is something you find along the way. Notice that the verses hold both verbs: I will give you rest, and ye shall find rest. Christians who stress either one are quoting the same lines. And the words of the promise are older than Matthew. Jeremiah, in the King James: "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls."
screen: `COME, ALL YE THAT LABOR.` · `REST AS A GIFT: I WILL GIVE YOU.` · `REST AS A PATH: LEARN OF ME.` · `GIVE AND FIND, IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, as if you've just set something down. Name one weight you're carrying this week, one task, one worry, one person you're holding up. For the length of the sit, leave it there in your open hands, and let someone else hold the other end of the beam.
Come unto me. The open door of Matthew 11: no test, no list, only tired people and an offer of rest.
Hold onto this: rest for your souls, given and found, under a yoke made for two. Be well.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray Matthew 11:28 at the end of a hard day, and in some churches the words come unto me are read aloud near communion as an invitation.

fork.setup: a friend says: rest is pure gift, you just come; the yoke part is extra. give the best case for the other side.
options: rest is earned: the harder you work, the more God gives you.
he says take my yoke and learn of me: rest is found walking his way.
the yoke means church rules, and rest comes once you keep them all.
fork.reveal: the strongest case for the second reading quotes the text itself: take my yoke, and learn of me, and ye shall find rest. the first reading quotes the line before it: I will give you rest. both are in Matthew 11.

original.note: Greek: easy, good, kind. Matthew 11:30: my yoke is easy.

what a scholar hears: the Greek for easy, chrestos, also means kind; Luke 6:35 uses it of God, kind unto the unthankful.
recall: a crowd that won't join any tune

chat.says: Pop says a yoke is made for two. i'm doing concert + apps + work. quit something or push through?
options: Maybe neither: find who you're pulling with. Ask for help on one piece and learn a gentler pace.
Quit all you can. Jesus means rest is having no yoke on you at all, nothing to carry.
Push through alone. The yoke is easy if your faith is strong enough to carry it all.
chat.meaning: Jesus offers rest and a yoke at once: come, take my yoke, learn of me. A yoke is pulled with someone, not alone.

heavy laden.meaning: weighed down, carrying a heavy load

yoke.meaning: a wooden beam that lets working animals pull together

Jeremiah.meaning: a prophet of Israel whose book is in the Bible

notes: Debate shape: the two readings (rest as gift, 'I will give you rest'; rest found by taking the yoke and learning, 'ye shall find rest') are both presented as Christian readings, with no denomination named and neither ranked. Confirm they are fairly put.
'Christians read his offer in more than one way' introduces the two readings without a count or date.

The carry 'rest for your souls' matches Jeremiah 6:16 (KJV) word for word; Matthew 11:29 KJV reads 'rest unto your souls'. The teach says the words of the promise are older than Matthew; Matthew does not cite Jeremiah here. Confirm the link is fair.
The hook's description of a yoke is general background, not from the text.
Trapdoor: χρηστός in Matthew 11:30 and in Luke 6:35 ('kind'). Confirm the lexical link before shipping.

Grace storyline day 3: Grace is overloaded (concert, college applications, a job). Pop, her grandfather, appears through her text ('a yoke is made for two'). The right reply is to find help and a gentler pace, not to quit everything or push through alone.
Practice kind: a body posture (open hands). No 'if you pray' line.
